title: Subways: HUH! What are they good for?
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss the history and engineering of subways, drawing on a HowStuffWorks article by Tracy V. Wilson. They open with banter about New York subway navigation and the A Train, then cover subway systems in Paris, London, and New York, and the shift from horse-drawn omnibuses to underground transit. Construction methods are covered in depth: tunnel boring machines, the New Austrian tunneling method, cut-and-cover, dealing with aquifers and rivers, compressed-air work and the bends, and ground freezing with calcium chloride. Other topics include abandoned stations such as the Brooklyn Bridge loop, subway shelters during the Blitz and wartime, the Tokyo sarin attack and 9/11 damage to subways, electrification via third rails, keying-by signals, the geometry train that checks track alignment, subway car lifespans and disposal at sea, the Coney Island shop, ridership and cleanliness rankings, and Atlanta's MARTA. The episode ends with listener mail about a couple who bonded over the show.

segments.title: Opening banter and the A Train
segments.summary: The hosts open with banter about the A Train song and their experiences navigating the New York subway together.

segments.title: Subway systems of Paris, London and New York
segments.summary: They compare station density in Paris, the London Tube, and the New York subway, and note that the London Underground opened first in 1863, followed by the Paris Metro and then New York in 1904, all during the Industrial Revolution's urban growth.

segments.title: Horse-drawn omnibuses and the move underground
segments.summary: Above-ground transit used horses and omnibuses, which produced large amounts of manure, so cities turned to underground mass transit.

segments.title: Tunnel boring machines and early hand digging
segments.summary: Modern tunnel boring machines are contrasted with the hand-digging of early projects using picks, shovels and dynamite. Workers died in large numbers on New York projects, and the hosts discuss bedrock.

segments.title: New Austrian tunneling method and cut-and-cover
segments.summary: The New Austrian tunneling method is described as a collection of techniques. Cut-and-cover is explained as digging a trench in a street, building the subway, and then rebuilding the street above it.

segments.title: Obstacles, utility lines, aquifers and river tunneling
segments.summary: Obstacles such as utility lines and old pipes are discussed, along with hitting aquifers and tunneling under rivers. In Paris, compressed-air pods were used under water, and workers got the bends. Ground was frozen with calcium chloride to remove wet mud. Cut-and-cover was used under San Francisco Bay.

segments.title: Abandoned stations, quarries and the City Hall loop
segments.summary: Underground finds in Paris include catacombs and deep quarries. The hosts describe the loop on the six train near City Hall, which passes an abandoned stained-glass station, and discuss whether passengers can still get off there.

segments.title: Signals, electrification, geometry train and rail maintenance
segments.summary: Keying-by signals are described, followed by third rail electrification and the geometry train that uses lasers to check track alignment and extinguishes hot spots.

segments.title: Car lifespan, Coney Island shop, rankings, wartime and terror history
segments.summary: The hosts cover subway car lifespans and their disposal at sea, the Coney Island shop, cleanliness and ridership rankings, subway shelters in World War II, the Tokyo sarin attack, and the 2005 London attacks. They also discuss fares, MARTA in Atlanta, and the Q line.

segments.title: Listener mail: anniversary
segments.summary: A listener writes about her three-year anniversary, saying the show brought her and her boyfriend together.
